en: Majjhima Nikāya 138:
Uddesavibhaṅgasutta Thus have I heard—
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the exposition of the summary.”
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:

“Monks, a monk should examine things in such a way that, as he examines them, his consciousness is neither distracted nor scattered externally, is not fixed internally, and does not tremble due to lack of clinging.

Monks, when consciousness is not distracted or scattered externally, is not fixed internally, and does not tremble due to lack of clinging, there is no arising of the origin of suffering—namely, birth, aging, and death—in the future.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, it occurred to those bhikkhus:
"Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling after giving us a brief summary of the teaching without analyzing its meaning in detail."

“Monks, a monk should investigate in such a way that, as he investigates, his consciousness is neither distracted nor scattered externally, and it is not settled internally; thus, through non-clinging, he does not tremble.

Monks, when consciousness is not distracted or scattered externally, and is not settled internally, for one who does not tremble through non-clinging, there is no origination of the arising of suffering—of birth, aging, and death—in the future.”
“Who, indeed, might analyze in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning which has not yet been analyzed in detail?
Then it occurred to those bhikkhus:
“This venerable Mahākaccāna is praised and esteemed by the Teacher himself and by his wise fellow-celibates.”
“The Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail.
What if we were to approach the Venerable Mahākaccāna and, having approached him, question the Venerable Mahākaccāna about this matter?
Then those bhikkhus went to where the Venerable Mahākaccāna was, and having approached him, they exchanged greetings with the Venerable Mahākaccāna.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Venerable Mahākaccāna:
“Friend Kaccāna, the Blessed One, having given us this brief summary and without explaining the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling:”

“‘In whatever way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should investigate so that, as he investigates, his consciousness is neither distracted nor scattered externally, and being unestablished internally, he does not tremble because of clinging.

When consciousness is not distracted or scattered externally, and is unestablished internally, for one who does not tremble because of clinging, there is no origination of the future suffering of birth, aging, and death.
Then, friends Kaccāna, not long after the Blessed One had departed, this occurred to us:”
"Friends, having given us this brief summary and without analyzing the meaning in detail, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling, saying:

'In whatever way, monks, a bhikkhu should investigate, so that as he investigates, his consciousness is neither scattered nor diffused externally, and being unestablished internally, he does not tremble because of non-clinging.'"

“Bhikkhus, when consciousness is not distracted and not scattered externally, and is not settled internally, for one who does not cling and is not agitated, there is no origination of the future mass of suffering consisting in birth, aging, and death.
“Who, friend Kaccāna, might analyze in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning which has not yet been analyzed in detail?
It occurred to us, friends: [that we ourselves might do so].
‘This Venerable Mahākaccāna is indeed praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise fellow-celibates.
The Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed.
Suppose we were to approach the Venerable Mahākaccāna and, having approached him, question the Venerable Mahākaccāna regarding this matter.’
“Let the venerable Mahākaccāna explain it.
“Friend, it is just as if a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood,
were to pass right by a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, bypassing its root and bypassing its trunk, and look for heartwood in the branches and foliage.”

"Venerable sirs, it would be as if one who had met the Teacher face-to-face thought, 'I should ask this matter of someone else,' and thus, having bypassed the Blessed One, you think that you should ask us about this matter.

For, friends, that Blessed One knows what should be known and sees what should be seen; he is become vision, become knowledge, become the Dhamma, become the Brahma; he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the guide to the goal, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata."
"It was indeed the right time for you to have asked the Blessed One about this matter yourself;
you should have retained it exactly as the Blessed One would have explained it.

"Truly, friend Kaccāna, the Blessed One knows what should be known and sees what should be seen. He is become vision, become knowledge, become the Dhamma, become the Brahma. He is the speaker, the proclaimer, the guide to the goal, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata."
Indeed, it would have been the right time for us to ask the Blessed One about this matter ourselves,
so that we might have remembered it exactly as the Blessed One explained it.
Nevertheless, the Venerable Mahākaccāna is praised and esteemed by the Teacher and by his wise fellow-celibates.
“Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail.
May the venerable Mahākaccāna analyze it, not taking it as troublesome.
“Therefore, friends, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.”
“Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahākaccāna.
The Venerable Mahākaccāna said this:
“Friends, regarding that brief summary which the Blessed One recited and then, without explaining the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling:”

“Monks, a monk should examine things in such a way that, as he examines them, his consciousness is not distracted or scattered externally, nor settled internally; and by not grasping, he does not become agitated.
Monks, when consciousness is not distracted or scattered externally, and is not settled internally, by not grasping—”
‘For one who is not agitated, there is no arising of the origin of suffering consisting in future birth, aging, and death.
This, friends, is how I understand the detailed meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, which had not been explained in detail.
And how, friends, is consciousness said to be distracted and scattered externally?
Here, friends, when a bhikkhu has seen a form with the eye, his consciousness follows after the sign of the form, is attached to the gratification in the sign of the form,
is fettered by the gratification in the sign of the form, and is conjoined with the fetter of gratification in the sign of the form;
his consciousness is scattered externally, and this is called "distracted."
Having heard a sound with the ear … having smelled an odor with the nose … having tasted a flavor with the tongue …
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, there arises consciousness that pursues the sign of the mental phenomenon;

consciousness that is attached to gratification in the sign of the mental phenomenon, bound by gratification in the sign of the mental phenomenon, and fettered by the fetter of gratification in the sign of the mental phenomenon—this is external consciousness.
"Scattered" is said to mean "dispersed.
In this way, friends, consciousness is said to be scattered and dispersed externally.
And how, friends, is consciousness said to be unscattered and undispersed externally?
In this case, friends, when a bhikkhu has seen a form with the eye, his consciousness does not follow after the sign of the form;
it is not attached to the gratification in the sign of the form, not fettered by the gratification in the sign of the form, and not bound by the fetter of the gratification in the sign of the form.
His consciousness is said to be undistracted and unscattered externally.
Having heard a sound with the ear … having smelled an odor with the nose … having tasted a flavor with the tongue …
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, his consciousness does not follow after the sign of the phenomenon;

it is not attached to gratification in the sign of the phenomenon, not fettered by gratification in the sign of the phenomenon, and not bound by the fetter of gratification in the sign of the phenomenon, directed outwardly.
Consciousness is said to be undistracted and unscattered.
In this way, friends, consciousness is said to be undistracted and unscattered externally.
And how, friends, is it said to be established internally?

"Here, friends, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.

His consciousness follows after the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion; it is attached to the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, bound by the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, and fettered by the fetter of the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
This is called 'the mind is settled internally.'"

Furthermore, friends, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.

His consciousness follows after the rapture and happiness born of concentration; it is attached to the rapture and happiness born of concentration, bound by the rapture and happiness born of concentration, and fettered by the attachment to the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
This is called "the mind is settled internally."
Furthermore, friends, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells equanimous and mindful, clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body;
he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He dwells happily, mindful and equanimous."

His consciousness follows after equanimity; it is attached to the gratification of equanimity and happiness, bound by the gratification of equanimity and happiness, and fettered by the fetter of the gratification of equanimity and happiness. It is said that his mind is settled internally.

Furthermore, friends, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.

His consciousness follows after neither-pain-nor-pleasure; it is attached to the gratification in neither-pain-nor-pleasure, fettered by the gratification in neither-pain-nor-pleasure, and bound by the fetter of the gratification in neither-pain-nor-pleasure. This is called "the mind is not settled within.
In this way, friend, it is said that the mind is settled within.
And how, friend, is it said that the mind is not settled within?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna...
His consciousness does not follow after the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion;

it is not attached to the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, not fettered by the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, and not bound by the fetter of the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
It is said that his mind is not stuck internally.
Furthermore, friends, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna...
His consciousness does not follow after the rapture and pleasure born of concentration, nor is it attached to the gratification in the rapture and pleasure born of concentration.

The mind is said to be unestablished when it is not bound by attachment to the rapture and pleasure born of concentration, nor fettered by the fetter of attachment to the rapture and pleasure born of concentration.
Furthermore, friends, with the fading away of rapture... [he] enters and dwells in the third jhāna.

His consciousness does not follow after equanimity; it is not attached to the gratification of equanimity and happiness, not fettered by the gratification of equanimity and happiness, and not bound by the fetter of the gratification of equanimity and happiness. Thus, his mind is said to be "not stuck internally.

Furthermore, friends, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.

His consciousness does not follow after neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; it is not attached to the gratification in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, not fettered by the gratification in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, and not bound by the fetter of the gratification in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Thus his mind is said to be "unestablished internally.
In this way, friend, it is said that the mind is unestablished internally.
And how, friends, does agitation arise through clinging?

Here, friends, an uninstructed worldling—who has no regard for the noble ones, is unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has no regard for true persons, is unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and undisciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as being in self, or self as being in form.
That form of his changes and becomes otherwise.
Due to that change and alteration of form, consciousness becomes preoccupied with the change of form.
The agitation born from being preoccupied with the change of form arises through the occurrence of mental phenomena and remains obsessing the mind.
Due to the obsession of the mind, one becomes fearful, distressed, and expectant, and one trembles with agitation because of non-clinging.
[The same applies to] feeling...
perception... [and so on].
He regards volitional formations as self, or self as possessing volitional formations, or volitional formations as in self, or self as in volitional formations.
That consciousness of his changes and becomes otherwise.
Due to the change and alteration of his consciousness, his consciousness becomes subject to that change and alteration.
The agitation born from being subject to the change and alteration of consciousness arises through the emergence of phenomena and remains obsessing the mind.
Because of this obsession of the mind, he becomes anxious, distressed, and longing; and without clinging, he trembles with fear.
In this way, friends, there is agitation due to clinging.
And how, friends, is there non-agitation due to non-clinging?

Here, friends, the well-taught noble disciple—who has seen the noble ones, is skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, and is well-disciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; who has seen true persons, is skilled in the Dhamma of true persons, and is well-disciplined in the Dhamma of true persons—[is not agitated].
One does not regard form as self, nor self as possessing form, nor form as being in self, nor self as being in form.
When that form of his changes and becomes otherwise,
his consciousness does not follow after the change and alteration of that form.
The agitation born of following the transformation of form, arising from phenomena, does not persist by obsessing the mind.
Because the mind is not obsessed, he is neither agitated, nor distressed, nor longing; and through non-clinging, he does not tremble.
[It is the same with] feeling…

One does not regard perception as self, nor the self as possessing perception, nor perception as being in the self, nor the self as being in perception; one does not regard volitional formations as self... nor consciousness as self, nor the self as possessing consciousness, nor consciousness as being in the self, nor the self as being in consciousness.
That consciousness of his changes and becomes otherwise.
Because that consciousness changes and becomes otherwise, his consciousness does not follow after the change of consciousness.
Thus, the agitation born from following after the change of consciousness does not arise in him, and the states produced by that do not remain obsessing his mind.
Through the complete transcendence of the mind, one is neither overwhelmed by taints, nor afflicted, nor expectant; and by not grasping, one does not tremble.
In this way, friends, there is non-trembling through non-grasping.
Now, friends, regarding that brief summary which the Blessed One recited and then, without explaining the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling:

“Monks, a monk should investigate in such a way that, as he investigates, his consciousness is neither distracted nor scattered externally, and it is not settled internally; thus, through non-clinging, he does not tremble.

Monks, when consciousness is not distracted or scattered externally, and is not settled internally, for one who does not tremble through non-clinging, there is no origination of the future suffering of birth, aging, and death.”
"Friends, regarding this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail, I understand its meaning in detail in this way.
However, if you wish, venerable friends, you should approach the Blessed One himself and inquire about this matter;
as the Blessed One explains it to you, so should you remember it."
Then those bhikkhus, having rejoiced and expressed their appreciation for the Venerable Mahākaccāna’s words, rose from their seats and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, when the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling after giving us this brief summary without explaining the meaning in detail:

‘Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should examine things in such a way that, as he examines them, his consciousness is not distracted or scattered externally, nor settled internally, and by not clinging, he does not become agitated.’”

“Bhikkhus, when consciousness is not distracted and not scattered externally, and is not established internally, for one who does not cling and is not agitated, there is no origination of the future suffering of birth, aging, and death.
Then, Bhante, not long after the Blessed One had departed, this occurred to us:
“Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling after giving us this brief summary without explaining the meaning in detail.”

"In whatever way, monks, a monk should investigate so that, as he investigates, his consciousness is neither distracted nor scattered externally, and being unestablished internally, he does not tremble because of non-clinging.

Monks, when consciousness is undistracted and unscattered externally, and is unestablished internally, for one who does not tremble due to non-clinging, there is no origination of the arising of suffering—of birth, aging, and death—in the future."
"Who might be able to analyze in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail?
Then, venerable sir, it occurred to us:
"This venerable Mahākaccāna is praised and esteemed by the Teacher himself and by his wise fellow-celibates."
“The Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail.

What if we were to approach the Venerable Mahākaccāna and inquire about this matter? Then, venerable sir, we approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna and, having approached him, inquired about this matter.
“Venerable sir, the meaning has been analyzed for us by the Venerable Mahākaccāna in these ways, with these phrases, and with these syllables.
“Bhikkhus, Mahākaccāna is wise; Mahākaccāna has great wisdom.
If you had questioned me about this matter, I too would have answered exactly as it was answered by Mahākaccāna.”
"This, indeed, is its meaning. And you should remember it thus.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Elated, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Uddesavibhaṅgasutta, the eighth, is finished.
